source.title: Improving Dictionary Learning with Gated Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Senthooran Rajamanoharan; Arthur Conmy; Lewis Smith; Tom Lieberum; Vikrant Varma; J'anos Kram'ar; Rohin Shah; Neel Nanda

record.tranche_reason: The study trains and evaluates sparse autoencoders on language-model activations, reporting sparse reconstruction and human interpretability results relevant to whether SAE dictionaries recover useful features. It does not test the original toy-model interventions or feature geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports numerous SAE training and ablation comparisons. They bear on SAE training quality, but not directly on whether real model features are canonical, causally meaningful units. The authors explicitly say their evaluations do not test whether learned dictionaries contain causally meaningful intermediate variables.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It introduces Gated SAEs and benchmarks them against baseline SAEs on L0, loss recovered, shrinkage and paired human interpretability. Every reported result compares the authors' own dictionary-learning method with another one. The paper does not ask whether LLM activations contain recoverable sparse features (V4), nor whether SAE features are canonical (V5). The authors say their evaluations do not test causal validity, and that SAE work assumes sparsity and linearity. Superposition serves as motivation, and SAEs as a tool.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that Gated SAEs Pareto-improve the sparsity–fidelity trade-off, and at many sites need about half the L0 for the same loss recovered. They also resolve shrinkage and are comparably interpretable, though not demonstrably more so. Every key part of the method was needed in ablations. They caution that SAE work rests on sparsity and linearity assumptions, and that they did not test whether learned dictionaries contain causally meaningful variables.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops and evaluates Gated Sparse Autoencoders, a modification of SAE dictionary learning, rather than reproducing the original toy-network superposition method. It separates feature gating from magnitude estimation and changes the training loss.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with sparsity level (L0), model, site, and layer. The paper reports interpretability differences across sites and layers and an evaluation anomaly at Gemma-7B layer 27 attention output pre-linear.

fits_no_version.finding: The L1-trained baseline SAEs show shrinkage (γ<1). Gated SAEs remove it (γ≈1) in GELU-1L and Pythia-2.8B. Fixing shrinkage alone explains only a small part of the Gated advantage.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE training objectives bias the learned dictionary and its activations: feature directions recovered depend on the architecture and loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Decoder quality judged by inference-time optimisation differs with training sparsity. The best baseline dictionary (L0≈99) is comparable to the best Gated one (L0≈20).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dictionary quality depends on training hyperparameters, a methodological sensitivity of SAE-based feature recovery.

record.problems: The study evaluates SAE reconstruction and human-rated interpretability rather than causal validity or completeness of recovered features. Human interpretability results are inconclusive and subjective; the paper reports rater and site/layer variation. Some Gemma-7B evaluation results exceed 1.0 because of a dataset mismatch and mean-ablation effect.
record.rows_left_out: The paper includes many per-run L0 and loss-recovered entries in Tables 1–8 and plotted frontier points in Figures 5, 12, and 13. These individual training configurations are not transcribed; rows summarize the authors' reported aggregate comparisons and include the stated evaluation anomaly.

untested.parts: All of V1. The Appendix F toy model is a one-dimensional illustration of Jump ReLU vs ReLU encoders; the authors say it was never empirically tested.
The paper never frames a test of whether LLMs contain sparse, dictionary-recoverable features. Absolute reconstruction numbers in Tables 1–8 exist only as SAE benchmarks.
Completeness, stability, canonicity and causal meaningfulness of SAE features. The authors say their evaluations do not test causal meaningfulness.
All of V6. Features are defined as linear directions by construction.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and V4 'supports' labels mistake a method benchmark for a test of the claim. The tables do report high absolute loss recovered at low L0, e.g. Gemma-7B layer-6 residual Gated SAE at L0 14.3 with 99.35% CE recovered. Human raters also labelled many features interpretable (Figure 7). These could serve as weak indirect V4 evidence, but the paper presents them only to compare SAE variants. Appendix H shows interpretability differences vary by site: MLP outputs show a significant Gated advantage, while attention and residual SAEs do not. This bears on the method, not on the claim.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network superposition, feature overlap and orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometric arrangements.
Whether neuron polysemanticity results from limited capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Alternative causes of polysemantic neurons and whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
The study evaluates SAE decompositions of activations in Pythia-2.8B and Gemma-7B, but does not establish that the recovered features are the model's actual internal units or validate them causally.
Completeness, stability, and canonical status of SAE features.
Whether model features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional subspaces.

rows.subject: Pythia-2.8B
rows.operation_detail: Compared Gated and baseline SAE sparse reconstruction and loss-recovered Pareto frontiers across tested sites and layers.

conditions.value: MLP outputs, attention outputs pre-linear, and residual stream post-MLP
Gated SAEs versus baseline SAEs; equal training compute

rows.measure: L0 sparsity and loss recovered (reconstruction fidelity)
rows.baseline: Baseline SAEs; no single numerical reference stated for the aggregate comparison.
rows.value: At all sites tested, Gated SAEs are a Pareto improvement; in every plot the SAE with maximal loss recovered was a Gated SAE.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative result across the plotted sites and layers; individual frontier points and table entries are not transcribed here.
rows.check: This row compares the study's own method with a baseline: Gated vs baseline SAE Pareto frontiers in Pythia-2.8B. A relative advantage of one SAE architecture does not measure whether sparse features exist in the model. It should not be linked to V4.

rows.subject: Gemma-7B
rows.operation_detail: Compared Gated and baseline SAE sparse reconstruction and loss-recovered Pareto frontiers across tested sites and layers.

conditions.value: MLP outputs, attention outputs pre-linear, and residual stream post-MLP
Gated SAEs versus baseline SAEs; equal training compute

rows.measure: L0 sparsity and loss recovered (reconstruction fidelity)
rows.baseline: Baseline SAEs; no single numerical reference stated for the aggregate comparison.
rows.value: The paper reports Pareto-frontier comparisons in Figure 13. At the attention output pre-linear site at layer 27, loss recovered is bigger than 1.0; the authors attribute this to the evaluation dataset differing from Gemma's pretraining data and mean ablation lowering loss at that site.
rows.locator: Appendix B, Figure 13 and accompanying discussion
rows.note: The reported layer-27 attention-site anomaly makes this comparison dependent on evaluation conditions; the text does not state a single aggregate numerical advantage for all Gemma sites.
rows.check: This is a method comparison in Gemma-7B. The value also misstates the text: Appendix B says Gated SAEs outperform baseline at all but one MLP output or residual-stream site. The loss recovered above 1.0 at the layer-27 attention site is an evaluation artifact (dataset mismatch; mean ablation lowers loss). It does not limit any claim version.

rows.subject: Pythia-2.8B SAE features
rows.operation_detail: Blind human ratings of randomly sampled baseline and Gated SAE features; paired by model, layer, site, and rater.
rows.measure: Mean difference in interpretability labels, with No=0, Maybe=1, Yes=2
rows.note: The study does not provide a model-specific point estimate in the text; its authors say the data do not establish that Gated features are more interpretable.
rows.check: This is a Gated-minus-baseline interpretability difference: a method comparison whose CI [−.07, .33] includes zero. It measures relative interpretability between two SAE types, not whether the model's features are sparse and recoverable.

rows.subject: Gemma-7B SAE features
rows.operation_detail: Blind human ratings of randomly sampled baseline and Gated SAE features; paired by model, layer, site, and rater.
rows.measure: Mean difference in interpretability labels, with No=0, Maybe=1, Yes=2
rows.note: One rater rated two features each and the others one each from baseline or Gated SAEs at each tested site-layer pair.
rows.check: This is the same kind of method comparison for Gemma-7B (CI [−.04, .29]). It is not a measure of any version.

rows.subject: Pythia-2.8B and Gemma-7B SAE features
rows.operation_detail: Paired blind human ratings of sampled baseline and Gated SAE features, pooled across both models.
rows.measure: Mean difference in interpretability labels, with No=0, Maybe=1, Yes=2
rows.value: Estimate .13; p = .060; the authors conclude the features are at least comparable in interpretability, but they cannot conclude Gated features are more interpretable.
rows.note: This is the reported pooled result; the paper notes subjective variation among raters and differences across sites and layers.
rows.check: This is the pooled method comparison (estimate .13, p = .060). It is not a measure of any version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Pythia-2.8B, tested SAE sites and layers
reader_labels.reason: Gated and baseline SAE results show sparse reconstructions with a Pareto improvement for Gated SAEs across tested sites; this is indirect evidence that SAE dictionaries can recover sparse decompositions (r1).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Human-rated SAE features in Pythia-2.8B and Gemma-7B
reader_labels.reason: Ratings support at least comparable interpretability, but do not establish that learned features are complete or actual model units; model-specific comparisons are inconclusive (r3, r4, r5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope

reader_labels.reason: The paper reports an evaluation anomaly at this site and does not state a single aggregate numerical advantage across all Gemma sites (r2).
